🔥 Hong Kong Fire 2025

Photo: Tyrone Siu/Reuters.

A catastrophic fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po, Hong Kong, engulfed seven of eight residential towers on November 26, 2025 — the city's deadliest fire since 1948. Authorities cite gross negligence in renovation works as a key driver of the blaze and its rapid spread. This hub is the entry point; the detail lives on the pages linked below.

📄  THE INDEPENDENT COMMITTEE REPORT — released 29 October 2026
Two volumes · 16 chapters · 1,000+ pages. Published with certain parts redacted (in the Index, Executive Summary and Chapters 4, 6 and 10–15) to avoid prejudicing the criminal prosecutions; the government bowed in apology and Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho resigned — the only official held to account. The full report is preserved in the archive in English and Chinese.
→ Read the full breakdown, page images & download the report »

At a glance

The fire26 Nov 2025, Wang Fuk Court, Tai Po. 168 dead, 79 injured; 7 of 8 towers burned — Hong Kong's deadliest fire since 1948.
CauseCigarettes in an air shaft most likely ignited non-compliant scaffold netting and foam boards; lead counsel told the inquiry that nearly all fire-safety systems failed "because of human factors". → Investigation
The inquiryJudge-led Independent Committee (David Lok) — 80 witnesses, 30 sessions; lead counsel's closing address said the government bore "unshirkable responsibility." Report submitted 22 Oct 2026.
The reportRedacted version published 29 Oct 2026 — certain parts redacted to avoid prejudicing the criminal prosecutions. → The Report & the Reckoning
AccountabilityCE John Lee and seven officials bowed in apology; Housing chief Winnie Ho resigned; the three other ministers over faulted departments are staying. Bereaved residents want all four out, and about 40–50 civil servants face a three-month investigation. → The Report & the Reckoning
Criminal case7 people + 2 firms (Prestige Construction, Will Power Architects) face 25 charges incl. manslaughter; next hearing 14 Jan 2027.
ReformsCriminalise bid-rigging, scrap and replace the ICU, a new Building Maintenance authority, and a Buildings Ordinance overhaul.
ResettlementHK$6.8b buyback; 99.1% accepted, 17 holdouts; a months-long fight for a homeowners' meeting. → Resettlement & Owners

Key Facts

  • Impact and scale: Fire began ~2:52 p.m. on Nov 26, 2025 at Wang Fuk Court, Tai Po (~2,000 flats/~4,600 residents; ~40% aged 65+). Seven of eight towers burned; 200 fire trucks, 100 ambulances, and >800 firefighters/paramedics deployed. Building fatalities: Wang Tai 82, Wang Cheong 70, Wang Sun 3, Wang Do 2, Wang Shing 1; none in Wang Yan/Wang Kin/Wang Chi; one victim not yet tied to a block (UDN/Ming Pao/TVBS/DotDotNews). SPCA estimates >537 animals affected; 364 found (294 survived, 70 died, 173 missing) (RTHK).
  • Materials and systems: Highly flammable polystyrene and foam panels blocked windows and escape routes; alarms found non-functional across all towers (some residents say alarms were switched off during works). Officials say 7 of 20 scaffold-net samples failed fire-resistance tests; allegations of mesh swapping to evade inspections (AP). Elevator-lobby windows reportedly sealed with foam boards; residents complained in 2024 about flammable netting/foam (NYT). PolyU’s Xinyan Huang later clarified remarks on bamboo’s role and urged caution pending a full technical study.

Explore the collection

  • In Memoriam — In Memoriam: the 168 people killed, by name.
  • Timeline — the full chronology, from the blaze to the report and its aftermath.
  • Investigation — what caused the fire and spread, the materials and evidence, and who the inquiry faulted.
  • The Report & the Reckoning — the Independent Committee report, the apology, the reforms, and preserved copies of all six volumes.
  • Resettlement & Owners — the buyback, the 17 holdouts, rehousing, and the homeowners'-meeting fight with administrator Hop On.
  • People — victims and residents, responders, officials, experts, the accused, and whistleblowers.
  • Activism — vigils and mourning, solidarity and donations, and the suppression of dissent.

References

  • Resettlement and displaced residents: AP (Hong Kong fire victims long for home as Lunar New Year stirs painful memories).
  • Spread and materials: Reuters graphic (How the deadly Hong Kong inferno spread); BBC visual explainer (How the Hong Kong fire spread); CNN visual timeline (How the blaze escalated within hours).
  • Background and complaints: NYT pre-fire warnings (Officials warned a year before the fire); FactWire building-maintenance bid database (FactWire archive); GitHub “Hong Kong Fire Documentary” (repo).
  • Governance and response: WSJ on information control and judge-led committee (WSJ); HKEJ on URA scoring (HKEJ); AP on netting tests and project suspensions (AP); UN rights chief urging Hong Kong to drop cases against those demanding an independent inquiry and warning of shrinking civic space (UN News).
  • Condolences and tributes: NHK, Focus Taiwan, EEAS, TRT World, Royal Household, Tehran Times, Korea JoongAng Daily, Arab News, Korea Herald, HKFP roundup.

noteIndex.body:
[![Great Extinction](/assets/extinctions.jpeg)](/notes/wx39zljncctue32jn06u29u/) 
> (_Courtesy: [Hong Kong Freepress](https://hongkongfp.com/2021/11/28/explainer-over-50-groups-gone-in-11-months-how-hong-kongs-pro-democracy-forces-crumbled/), 2021_) 

SHKO (Save Hong Kong Online) is a community-driven project dedicated to preserving the rapidly disappearing websites and online resources of Hong Kong’s civil society and independent media since 2019. In response to the sweeping shutdowns caused by political changes in Hong Kong, we aim to safeguard digital heritage before it vanishes. This project is anonymous, open source, and supported by a global network of contributors.

While most sites in our archive were forced offline due to Hong Kong’s political deterioration, it’s important to note that [[RFA Cantonese|sites.rfa_cantonese]] is the only site here closed not because of Hong Kong’s situation, but due to internal political decisions in the United States.

Explore our full list of preserved sites and archives on the [Collections page](/notes/wx39zljncctue32jn06u29u/).

Recent work: documenting the [[Hong Kong Fire 2025|hong-kong-fire-2025]] tragedy at Wang Fuk Court (168 dead, ongoing probes into flammable mesh/foam, bid-rigging, and a judge-led review), including activism, timeline, and investigation subpages; and the [[⚖️ Jimmy Lai case|faces-of-the-crackdown.jimmy-lai]] — Apple Daily founder sentenced to 20 years under the National Security Law (Feb 2026), with coverage of press freedom impact and international response; and [[🎵 Glory to Hong Kong|glory-to-hong-kong]] — the 2019 protest anthem and the 2024 court order that made it the first song banned in Hong Kong since the 1997 handover; and [[📕 Book Censorship under the NSL|book-censorship]] — how Hong Kong criminalised the printed word, from the banned Sheep Village children's-book trilogy (whose speech-therapist authors were jailed for sedition) and purged public libraries to the 2026 bookshop raids; and [[🗽 Statues & Monuments|statues]] — how Hong Kong's public monuments to Tiananmen and the 2019 protests (the Pillar of Shame, the Goddess of Democracy, Lady Liberty) were removed, seized as police evidence, and driven into exile abroad; and [[⚖️ The Hong Kong 47|hong-kong-47]] — the largest National Security Law case, in which 45 pro-democracy figures were jailed for up to 10 years over a 2020 opposition primary election; and [[🕯️ Tiananmen Vigil|tiananmen-vigil]] — the thirty-year Victoria Park candlelight vigil for the 1989 crackdown, the largest June 4th commemoration on Chinese soil, now banned and its organisers jailed; and [[✊ Faces of the Crackdown|faces-of-the-crackdown]] — a human index to the publishers, students, unionists and clergy jailed, exiled or tried under the National Security Law; and [[🎬 Films & Documentaries|films]] — the protest movement on film, a decade of documentaries and features (Ten Years, Revolution of Our Times, the Joshua Wong doc) now largely banned or unshowable in Hong Kong, gathered with their trailers; and [[📰 Press Freedom under Siege|press-freedom]] — how one of Asia's freest presses was dismantled in five years, from the raids that closed Apple Daily and Stand News to the revived sedition law now reaching lone online reporters.

## Goals
- To preserve as much information as possible before its disappearance during Hong Kong's great transition
- To illustrate a viable method that everyone can use to help preserve online heritage with no pains
- To demonstrate global collaborations to save local digital heritages with best practices

## Quick Facts

We are working on over dozens of [[websites or online causes | sites]] in Hong Kong in the past two decades which has been forced to shutdown or at the brink of disappearing. We'd welcome anyone help [[contribute | participation]] to the content and/or [[sponsor | sponsorship]] our program to sustain it together. 

Examples:
- [[sites.appledaily]] (Extincted)
- [[sites.inmediahk]] (In Danger)
